title: Motion of a Freely Falling Body
topicTitle: Motion of a freely falling body
notes: **Definition:** A freely falling body is an object moving under the influence of gravity alone, with no air resistance. Near Earth's surface, the acceleration is approximately constant: g = 9.8 m/s² downward.
**Equations for downward motion (dropped from rest):** If an object is released from rest (u = 0), the equations simplify: v = gt, h = ½gt², v² = 2gh. Here v is downward speed, h is distance fallen.

**Equations for upward motion (thrown upward):** When a body is thrown upward with initial speed u, gravity acts downward: v = u - gt, h = ut - ½gt², v² = u² - 2gh. Here h is height above launch point, v is velocity (positive upward).
**Time to reach maximum height:** At the top of the trajectory, v = 0. From v = u - gt, 0 = u - gt_up → t_up = u/g. The body is momentarily at rest at the maximum height.

**Total time of flight (launch and return to same level):** The body goes up and comes back down to the launch level. The time to go up equals the time to fall down from rest from height H. Total time T = 2u/g.
**Maximum height reached:** H = u²/(2g). This is derived from v² = u² - 2gH with v = 0 at the top. Height scales with the square of the initial speed — double the speed gives four times the height.

**Velocity when returning to launch level:** The body returns with the same speed u but opposite direction: v = -u. This is because gravity is a conservative force and mechanical energy is conserved (ignoring air resistance).

**Effect of air resistance:** In reality, air resistance opposes motion. A light object (feather) reaches terminal velocity quickly. A heavy dense object (coin) approximates free fall better. Terminal velocity v_t = √(2mg/(ρAC_d)) for quadratic drag.
**Galileo's inclined plane experiment:** Galileo couldn't measure free fall directly (too fast), so he used inclined planes with small angles to slow down the motion, establishing s ∝ t².

**Variation of g with height:** At height h above Earth's surface, g(h) = g_0(R/(R+h))², where R is Earth's radius (~6400 km). At ISS altitude (400 km), g ≈ 8.7 m/s² (11% less than surface). For most problems, g is treated as constant.

**Sign convention in free fall:** Choose a coordinate system and stick to it. Convention 1: Upward positive → a = -g. Convention 2: Downward positive → a = +g. Both work if applied consistently. The choice affects the signs of u, v, h, t.
confusion: A freely falling body does NOT have constant velocity — it has constant ACCELERATION (g). The velocity increases continuously: v = gt (if dropped) or v = u - gt (if thrown up). Many students confuse 'acceleration is constant' with 'velocity is constant'.

The mass of the object does NOT affect free fall acceleration (ignoring air resistance). A 1 kg mass and a 1000 kg mass fall with the same acceleration g. This was demonstrated by Galileo (allegedly at the Leaning Tower) and famously by Apollo 15 astronauts on the Moon.

At the top of the trajectory, the velocity is ZERO but the acceleration is STILL g downward. Many students think acceleration is zero at the top because velocity is zero. The acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; it does not vanish when velocity momentarily becomes zero.
The time to go up is NOT equal to the time to fall down if the landing level is different from the launch level. The t_up = t_down symmetry only holds for return to the SAME horizontal level.

Air resistance makes heavier objects fall faster in reality. A feather and a hammer dropped in vacuum fall at the same rate (as shown on the Moon). In air, the feather's terminal velocity is much lower due to its large surface-to-mass ratio.
practice: A stone is dropped from a 100 m tall cliff. (a) How long does it take to reach the ground? (b) What is its velocity just before impact? Solution: u = 0, h = 100 m, g = 9.8 m/s². (a) h = ½gt² → t = √(2h/g) = √(200/9.8) = √20.4 = 4.52 s. (b) v = gt = 9.8 × 4.52 = 44.3 m/s downward. Or v = √(2gh) = √(2×9.8×100) = 44.3 m/s.

A ball is thrown upward with speed 25 m/s. Find (a) maximum height, (b) time to reach top, (c) time to return to launch level, (d) velocity 3 seconds after launch. Solution: g = 9.8. (a) H = u²/(2g) = 625/19.6 = 31.9 m. (b) t_up = u/g = 25/9.8 = 2.55 s. (c) T = 2t_up = 5.10 s. (d) v = u - gt = 25 - 9.8×3 = 25 - 29.4 = -4.4 m/s (moving downward at 4.4 m/s).

A rock is thrown downward from a 50 m high bridge with an initial speed of 10 m/s. Find (a) time to hit the water, (b) impact velocity. Solution: Downward positive, u = 10, h = 50, g = 9.8. (a) 50 = 10t + ½(9.8)t² → 4.9t² + 10t - 50 = 0. t = [-10 + √(100 + 980)]/(9.8) = (-10 + √1080)/9.8 = (-10 + 32.86)/9.8 = 22.86/9.8 = 2.33 s. (b) v = u + gt = 10 + 9.8×2.33 = 32.8 m/s.

A stone is dropped from a balloon rising at 5 m/s at a height of 80 m. Find time to reach the ground and impact velocity. Solution: Balloon rising means stone has initial velocity u = -5 m/s (upward). h = -80 m (displacement downward). -80 = -5t + ½(-9.8)t² → 4.9t² + 5t - 80 = 0. t = [-5 + √(25 + 1568)]/9.8 = (-5 + 39.9)/9.8 = 34.9/9.8 = 3.56 s. v = u + gt = -5 + (-9.8)(3.56) = -5 - 34.9 = -39.9 m/s (downward).

A parachutist falls freely for 30 s before opening parachute. Find (a) speed after 30 s free fall, (b) distance fallen in 30 s. (Ignore air resistance during free fall.) Solution: (a) v = gt = 9.8 × 30 = 294 m/s. (b) h = ½gt² = 0.5 × 9.8 × 900 = 4410 m = 4.41 km. Note: Real terminal velocity with air resistance is ~50 m/s, not 294 m/s.
universalFacts: The value of g = 9.8 m/s² is an average at Earth's surface. It varies with latitude (higher at poles: 9.83 m/s², lower at equator: 9.78 m/s² due to rotation and Earth's oblate shape) and altitude.

Free fall is the classic example of constant acceleration motion. All objects in a vacuum fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass — this is the equivalence principle, which led Einstein to general relativity.
The period of a simple pendulum of length L is T = 2π√(L/g). Measuring T and L gives g. This was the standard method for measuring g before modern gravimeters.

In free fall, the object is weightless — the normal force is zero. This is why astronauts in orbit (which is continuous free fall) experience weightlessness. They are not outside Earth's gravity; they are falling with it.
The distance fallen in the nth second of free fall (from rest) is s_n = g(n - ½). This 'odd numbers rule' (1, 3, 5, 7... in units of g/2) was discovered by Galileo and used to prove s ∝ t².
